newsitem.title: UK: Copper market puzzles over post-Sumitomo rally.
newsitem.headline: Copper market puzzles over post-Sumitomo rally.

text.p: Copper prices on Wednesday powered to the highest levels since being toppled by the Sumitomo affair last year, but the market puzzled whether the rally was on solid ground.
Some players thought the spectre of Yasuo Hamanaka may still be haunting the market.
Others were certain China had taken his place as a huge buyer, soaking up a surplus of metal.
"Are we still seeing the aftershocks of those Sumitomo positions? Maybe we are," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
"Prices are not feeding off the fundamentals of the market. There are a lot of confusing signals," he added.

Copper's burst of strength on Wednesday, which took three month prices $74 higher to $2,360 per tonne, came two days after Hamanaka pleaded guilty to forgery and fraud charges in the world's biggest financial scandal.
News from Sumitomo last June that it had uncovered a web of unauthorised trades by Hamanaka sparked a panicky crash to $1,745, down nearly $1,000 from the year's peak.
Sumitomo, a huge supplier of physical copper, says it has so far lost $2.6 billion from Hamanaka's highly risky plays.

Some analysts last year suggested the departure of Hamanaka -- nicknamed Mr. Five Percent for the share of the world's copper market he was thought to control -- would allow a fundamental surplus to come to the fore as a slew of new mines gear up for output.
Only last week at an industry gathering in New York, analysts were debating how great a surplus the market would see this year.
Estimates ranged from 75,000 tonnes to more than 300,000 tonnes, probably concentrated at the end of the year.
But copper for immediate delivery remains in short supply as the market enters a peak demand period from March to June.
"The market still seems to be tight with stocks at relatively low levels," said analyst Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff.
London Metal Exchange inventories fell on Tuesday by 1,100 tonnes to 220,625 tonnes.
This is above the six-year low of 90,050 tonnes seen late last November but well under the 1996 peak of 356,800 tonnes and the more than 600,000 tonnes in early 1994.
A key uncertainty is the size of China's appetite for copper.
Some traders said Wednesday's rise was partly fuelled by rumours that Beijing had started piling into the market to replenish its strategic reserve.

"If the widespread rumours are anything like correct, the Chinese Strategic Reserve Board (SRB) has apparently been authorised to add several hundreds of thousands of tonnes to its stockpile over the 1996-2000 five year plan period," said Peter Hollands of consultancy Bloomsbury Minerals Economics Ltd. in a recent report.
This Chinese buying would likely soak up any looming surplus, keeping cash prices in a 90-110 cents per lb ($1,984-$2,425 per tonne) range until about 1999, Hollands said.
Merrill Lynch metals analyst Ted Arnold recently boosted his estimate for cash LME copper by 7.5 cents/lb ($165/tonne) to 100 cents ($2,205) this year and 95 cents ($2,094) in 1998.
"We think the SRB will absorb the bulk of this year's surplus as 1997 and 1998 look to be years of high consumption within China," he said.
The market was likely to remain heated and nervous until it saw firm proof of a surplus, analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton said.
"Until the market sees evidence of stocks arriving, it will remain twitchy and susceptible to volatile moves," he said.
